The State's Legal War

By: Este de Klerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What picture emerges from the litany of recent judgments going against the president, his top ministers and parliament? What does it say when our highest courts need to take matters in hand?

Unique Selling Point:
What picture emerges from the litany of recent judgments going against the president, his top ministers and parliament? What does it say when our highest courts need to take matters in hand to force the top executive - President Jacob Zuma, his Cabinet, the National Authority of Parliament to do what they are actually just supposed to do being in those positions? Why is it necessary for any political party or labour union or civil society to go to court to ask judges to rule and make it a court order to see change?
The last 18 months have seen several judgments going against decisions made by pres. Jacob Zuma, his top ministers and Parliament. In many of these cases, the courts have ordered the president, parliament and ministers to do their jobs - and often even ordered them to pay up for the legal costs too. We sketch the big picture of the cumulative effect of these judgments and look at the implications of such judgments being delivered against the state.

With President Jacob Zuma's future seriously hanging in the balance and the President meeting with the the ANC's top six officials over his future this coming weekend, it adds to speculation that President Zuma could be removed as head of state.
This is exactly where these judgments delivered against the state are even more significant - because they all happened under Zuma's watch and many were delivered directly against him or against decisions he acted on.

We look at some of the major judgments in which the highest levels of the executive, like the Presidency and Parliament, has been lambasted in over the last 18 months and the consequences of these playing out at the moment. In many of these cases, the state has also launched appeal after appeal, driving up the costs even further. We will estimate the costs of these cases to the state, and ultimately to the taxpayer.

Summary:
The state is by far the biggest litigant in our courts. Hundreds of cases are ongoing against national, provincial and local government departments and at any given time.

But in the last year and a half, the highest levels of the state, such as the president and parliament, has been lambasted in certain high level cases about their behaviour and ordered to take steps to remedy it. The court’s have also taken the executive to task when it litigates “recklessly” with no chance of success.

While briefly referencing cases such as the Al-Bashir matter and the nuclear procurement matter, we will unpack the following cases to illustrate how the state has been slammed by the country’s highest courts and the consequences for the state.

In edit we will use a clever editing device to move from one case to the next.
Links will also be cleverly scripted before the shoot to naturally flow from one point/court case into the next. We will look at the following cases in detail.

1. The review of the Public Protector’s State Capture report, ConCourt, December 2017
2. The Nkandla Judgment, ConCourt, April 2016, and the subsequent Impeachment Judgment, Concourt, December 2017
3. 3. The Sassa social grants case, Concourt, March 2017 and the inquiry currently underway
4. The NPA/Mxolisi Nxasana judgement, High Court, December 2017



Further information:
We will report on the latest developments in each of these matters: (also see more details below)

1. Most recently, the review of the Public Protector’s State Capture report, ConCourt, December 2017, in which the president was lambasted for abusing the judicial process.

2. What could be seen as the beginning of the executive’s legal problems, the Nkandla Judgment, ConCourt, April 2016, and the subsequent Impeachment Judgment, Concourt, December 2017

3. The Sassa social grants case, in which the Constitutional Court felt obliged to appoint itself as nanny to supervise the entire process through which social grants payments would be taken over by Sassa itself after the court declared the contract with CPS invalid. The ConCourt also ordered an inquiry to be held into the social grants debacle, which is currently underway.

4. The NPA/Mxolisi Nxasana judgement, in which the High Court in Pretoria said in December 2017 that prosecutions boss Shaun Abrahams must vacate his seat. The court found that the termination of former prosecutions boss Mxolisi Nxasana’s contract was invalid and therefore, Shaun Abrahams’ appointment was also invalid. The court ruled that a new prosecutions boss should be appointed within 60 days. It also said that pres. Jacob Zuma could not make the appointment, as he was compromised due to the pending corruption charges against him. Instead, deputy president Cyril Ramaphosa was ordered to make the appointment. This decision is being appealed by the NPA and Shaun Abrahams.

We ask experts what it means when such judgments are delivered against the President, Parliament and national departments. What are the implications in terms of democracy and governance? What can be gleaned when you look at this as a trend rather than individual matters? What does it say about the behaviour of the state?

We also try to estimate the cost of these specific cases and subsequent appeals to the state, and ultimately the taxpayer.

Finally, we will try to give an overview of the sheer volume of cases the state has in the highest courts (Supreme Court of Appeal and Constitutional Court) and the costs that may be involved.

Further details of the cases to be highlighted:

REVIEW OF PUBLIC PROTECTOR’S STATE CAPTURE REPORT, NORTH GAUTENG HIGH COURT, DECEMBER 2017

In December 2017, the High Court in Pretoria delivered a blow to Zuma when it dismissed with costs his review of then Public Protector Thuli Madonsela’s recommended remedial action in her report on state capture. The court directed Zuma to carry out the remedial action set out by the Public Protector and appoint a commission on inquiry into state capture within 30 days. The inquiry was to be headed by a judge chosen by Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng.

The judgment lambasted Zuma for abusing the judicial process. The court said Zuma was “ill-advised and reckless in launching a challenge against the remedial action of the Public Protector”. It said Zuma’s conduct falls far short of the expectation on him as of the head of state to support institutions of democracy. It said he had no justifiable basis to ignore the impact of this corruption on the public and the Public Protector’s remedial action presented him with an opportunity to confront and address the problem, but instead his court challenge resulted in a further delay. “The failure to verify (former deputy finance minister) Mr (Mcebisi) Jonas' allegations (against the Guptas) may also have infringed the provisions of section 24 of the Prevention and Combating of Corrupt Activities Act. There is no evidence of action taken by anyone to verify (former ANC MP) Ms (Vytjie) Mentor's allegations,” the court said. The court also found that Zuma must personally carry the costs.

Zuma indicated his intention to appeal the judgment, but in the meantime (at the insistence of the ANC), he has appointed the commission of inquiry. Zuma has said he is taking further legal advice on his appeal plans. He may still go ahead with an appeal in an attempt to have the criticism against him reviewed.

Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo has been appointed to head up the commission and the terms of reference was published in the Government Gazette on 25 January. But Zuma has reportedly not yet signed the regulations without which the commission cannot start its work.

THE NKANDLA JUDGMENT/CONCOURT/APRIL 2016

A watershed, unanimous judgment of the Constitutional Court

WHAT HAPPENED:

In April 2016, the Constitutional Court handed down a precedent-setting judgment that both President Jacob Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations in the Nkandla matter.

"The president failed to uphold, defend, and respect the Constitution," Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng ruled.

Only a court of law could have set aside the Public Protector's findings and remedial action.

The Concourt found that President Jacob Zuma had acted inconsistently with the Constitution when he failed to comply with the former Public Protector, Thuli Madonsela's remedial action listed in her report on the upgrades to his Nkandla homestead.

The court ruled that President Zuma had to personally pay back the money for some of the upgrades, following a determination by the National Treasury.

The court also ruled that the National Assembly erred when it dismissed former Public Protector report. "The resolution by the National Assembly absolving the president from compliance with the Public Protector's remedial action is inconsistent with the Constitution, is invalid, and set aside," Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng said in his judgment.

Mogoeng said through a draft order President Zuma circulated eight days before the case was heard in the Constitutional Court, he showed that he accepted that the Public Protector's remedial action was binding.

The court ruled that President Zuma failed in his duty to help and protect the public protector’s office to ensure its independence, impartiality, dignity and effectiveness.


CONSEQUENCES:

This judgment was a victory for the Constitution and the rule of law. It showed that nobody was above the law, also not the President.

An important aspect of the judgment was that the Concourt had made declaratory orders that both President Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations. And the Concourt found it was duty-bound to rule on that.

The court ruled that President Zuma had to personally pay back the money for some of the upgrades, following a determination by the National Treasury.

Definite steps to determine how much Zuma should pay for the swimming pool, cattle kraal, chicken run, visitors' centre, and amphitheatre built at Nkandla.

The court ruled that the president must reprimand the ministers involved - as he said he would do in a draft order submitted to the court before the hearing in February, Zuma said he was willing to reprimand ministers, in line with the public protector’s remedial action.

The Constitutional Court made four orders relating to the repayment of some of the R246m spent on non-security upgrades at Nkandla. Firstly, National Treasury had to determine the reasonable cost of those features; namely the swimming pool, chicken run, cattle kraal, amphitheatre, and visitors’ centre. Secondly, it had to determine how much of this amount Zuma should pay. Treasury then had 60 days to report back to the court with its findings. Finally, Zuma then had 45 days to pay back the money. -

President Zuma, the National Assembly, and the Minister of Police had to pay the costs of the application, including the costs of two counsel.


The Nkandla matter still haunts pres. Jacob Zuma and Parliament. In December 2017, in an application by the EFF, UDM and COPE, the Constitutional Court found that the National Assembly had failed in its duties by not putting in place processes to hold the president accountable for his failure to implement the remedial action subscribed by the Public Protector in her report on the Nkandla security upgrades. The court found that the National Assembly breached the constitution and ordered it to make rules about the process mentioned in section 89 (1) of the Constitution, namely the process to impeach a president.

SASSA CASE, CONCOURT, MARCH 2017

In the Sassa social grants case, the Constitutional Court ordered the Department of Social Development to put systems in place to take over the payment of social grants from Cash Paymaster Services (CPS). This after the court declared the contract with CPS invalid. The department ignored the court’s first order in this regard, and after making a second order, the Constitutional Court felt it necessary to act uncharacteristically and appoint itself as a nanny to oversee the entire process. The department and Sassa was ordered to give the court regular process updates. Since then, Sassa finally, after many false starts, reached a deal with the Post Office to assist in distributing social grants.

The court ordered that an inquiry be held into the social grants debacle. The inquiry is ongoing, chaired by retired judge Bernard Ngoepe. The court also ordered Social Development Minister Bathabile Dlamini to personally carry the costs of the case, but she has submitted reasons why she should not be held personally liable.

NXASANA/NPA CASE, NORTH GAUTENG HIGH COURT, DECEMBER 2017

Press Release:


From the review of the Public Protector’s State of Capture report, to the Constitutional Court ruling that the National Assembly failed to hold president Jacob Zuma to account, the state is by far the biggest litigant in our courts. At any given time, there are hundreds of ongoing cases against national, provincial and local departments – and in many cases the government keeps losing. Justified litigation, or a taxpayers' burden?

Script:


VO: Over just 22 days in December, the country’s courts delivered three judgments scathing in their criticism of president Jacob Zuma and parliament. But these were just the latest in a long list.

DEVI LINK: Reckless, conflicted, in breach of constitutional obligations -- what does it mean when the courts use these words to describe a sitting president and his Ministers?

VO: Political analyst Aubrey Matshiqi.

AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: Every time a judgment goes against President Jacob Zuma, including the Nxasana matter, many things come to my mind, but foremost out of them is the extent to which his presidency has compromised our institutions.

VO: One of those institutions is the National Prosecuting Authority - and Zuma’s hiring and firing at the NPA led to one of the harshest judgments against him to date. He was heavily criticised for offering Mxolisi Nxasana a R17 million golden handshake to resign as prosecutions boss, and then appointing Shaun Abrahams.

DEVI LINK: Judge President of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Dunstan Mlambo ordered that Shaun Abrahams’ appointment was invalid and should be set aside, and that the next National Director of Public Prosecutions should be appointed by the deputy president.

(DATE STRAP: North Gauteng High Court, 8 December 2017) UPSOUND JUDGE DUNSTAN MLAMBO: In our view, President Zuma would be clearly conflicted in having to appoint a National Director of Public Prosecutions, given the background to which we have referred, particularly the many criminal charges against him that have not gone away.

VO: The corruption charges against Zuma date from the Arms Deal before he became president in 2009, and last year the Supreme Court of Appeal held that Abrahams should consider the charges anew.

DEVI LINK: The biggest question now is, what will happen once he’s no longer president -- will he finally have to answer in court to the litany of corruption charges he’s been fighting for a decade?

VO: Retired Constitutional Court Justice Johann Kriegler says Judge Mlambo’s judgment was a game changer.

JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: It made a credibility finding against the President. Now, that’s the first time that I am aware of that that has been so clearly decided in court.

VO: Retired Constitutional Court Justice Zak Yacoob believes cases like these come down to desperate scrambling by the president and his allies.

ZAK YACOOB, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: If you want to have an immoral government and a corrupt government every… no effort is lost in preserving that corrupt and immoral government because they won’t give up power and they will use state resources.

AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: You can’t appoint Mickey Mouse as your president and expect the state to perform like Albert Einstein.

VO: The other two judgments in December both related to Public Protector reports. In the Constitutional Court (DATE STRAP: Constitutional Court, 29 December 2017), 7 judges berated Parliament for failing to hold Zuma to account for his conduct related to the Nkandla report.

DEVI LINK: The significant and hard-hitting judgments against the national executive really started with the Nkandla judgment in this court nearly two years ago. It was the first time under our democracy that a court had such harsh words for a president.

VO: That was in March 2016, when the country’s highest court ordered Zuma to pay back the money spent on non-security upgrades. (DATE STRAP: Constitutional Court, 31 March 2016)

JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: It was the first real show of force, of muscle, by the Constitutional Court in saying to both the President and to Parliament, you’ve not done your job and you've got to do your job. That was a very, very significant case.

VO: In December, Judge Mlambo, also sent the president packing when he tried to fight the State of Capture report. Mlambo called the bid ill-advised and reckless. (DATE STRAP: North Gauteng High Court, 13 December 2017)

JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: If the courts use such strong language, it is an indication that there’s something wrong. It’s deplorable that such things have to be said but it’s commendable that they are being said.

VO: In the NPA case, Judge Mlambo berated Zuma for his tendency to appeal -- “... defending what ultimately turns out – on the president’s own concession – to have been indefensible all along, banking on any advantage that the passage of time may bring.” Zuma, Abrahams and the NPA are all appealing. Of course, the longer a case stays in court, the more expensive it becomes. And ultimately, it’s the taxpayer who coughs up millions.

AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: We’re talking about the amount of taxpayers’ monies that had been wasted when actors in the state, including the President have appealed to higher courts, sometimes to defend the indefensible.

VO: On any given day, there are hundreds of cases involving government departments in our courts, from claims for medical negligence and unlawful arrest to labour cases. In the last 6 months, the Office of the State Attorney received more than 2700 new cases. The budget for state legal services is R1.2 billion a year. But in high-profile cases, the president, parliament and ministers don’t use the State Attorney’s lawyers -- they hire expensive advocates in private practice.

JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: What is disturbing about it, is that many cases where the president personally or the minister personally is involved, the state pays those costs. That is of course wrong.

VO: Legal taxation experts say the bill for a team of advocates in a Constitutional Court case will be at least R1 million. This is the bill of a senior advocate who acted in the Constitutional Court in a case about the appointment of former Hawks head Berning Ntlemeza. It comes to just over R1 million. When the state loses, they must not only pay their own legal eagles, but usually also those of their opponents. In the 2016 Nkandla case, there were 11 advocates fighting the state’s case, and the state was also ordered to pay for 4 advocates for the EFF and DA. The cost would have been at least R15 million.

ZAK YACOOB, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: It’s a kind of double standards thing. The ANC would say, when they lose cases, people shouldn’t go to court and so on and so on, but they go to court often enough.

VO: Sometimes the courts do order government employees to pay the costs out of their own pockets. In December, Judge Mlambo ordered Zuma to pay up himself in both the NPA case and the review of the state capture report. The bill for all those advocates just to appear in the high court, would run to at least R1.9 million.

ZAK YACOOB, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: When they bring a case in the High Court and they lose, then go … take six months and go to the Supreme Court of Appeal, take another year and go the Constitutional Court and concede there, maybe in five years’ time, they’ll be ordered to pay. And then Zuma will go to his corrupt contacts who’ll form all sorts of linkages with all sorts of companies, and pay the costs.

VO: As South Africa grapples with an economy in trouble, it is untenable to keep paying these bills. The question remains: Where to from here?

JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: There has been an over-emphasis of the role of Mr Zuma in the bad place in which we find ourselves. I believe that there is much more involved in the capture of the nation than just Mr Zuma and his close associates.

AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: It is disappointing when you hear some ANC leaders saying the National Party was just as bad as if the National Party should be the standard by which we judge ourselves, whereas what we were fighting for is a society that would be the direct opposite, that would be the antithesis, of what apartheid society was.

PROMOS

10 secs
VO: Recently, government has suffered a series of heavy defeats in the country’s top courts, and no less than three in December. So, who’s paying for these losses?

15 secs
VO: What does it mean when the highest courts in the land deliver scathing judgments against the president and his top brass, even calling the president conflicted?
JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: It made a credibility finding against the President.

15 secs
VO: Who pays when the president and government keep suffering significant losses in the country’s courtrooms?
AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: The amount of taxpayers’ monies that had been wasted, sometimes to defend the indefensible.

Zuma indicated his intention to appeal the judgment, but in the meantime (at the insistence of the ANC), he has appointed the commission of inquiry. Zuma has said he is taking further legal advice on his appeal plans. He may still go ahead with an appeal in an attempt to have the criticism against him reviewed. Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo has been appointed to head up the commission and the terms of reference was published in the Government Gazette on 25 January. But Zuma has reportedly not yet signed the regulations without which the commission cannot start its work. THE NKANDLA JUDGMENT/CONCOURT/APRIL 2016 A watershed, unanimous judgment of the Constitutional Court WHAT HAPPENED: In April 2016, the Constitutional Court handed down a precedent-setting judgment that both President Jacob Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations in the Nkandla matter. "The president failed to uphold, defend, and respect the Constitution," Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng ruled. Only a court of law could have set aside the Public Protector's findings and remedial action. The Concourt found that President Jacob Zuma had acted inconsistently with the Constitution when he failed to comply with the former Public Protector, Thuli Madonsela's remedial action listed in her report on the upgrades to his Nkandla homestead. The court ruled that President Zuma had to personally pay back the money for some of the upgrades, following a determination by the National Treasury. The court also ruled that the National Assembly erred when it dismissed former Public Protector report. "The resolution by the National Assembly absolving the president from compliance with the Public Protector's remedial action is inconsistent with the Constitution, is invalid, and set aside," Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng said in his judgment. Mogoeng said through a draft order President Zuma circulated eight days before the case was heard in the Constitutional Court, he showed that he accepted that the Public Protector's remedial action was binding. The court ruled that President Zuma failed in his duty to help and protect the public protector’s office to ensure its independence, impartiality, dignity and effectiveness. CONSEQUENCES: This judgment was a victory for the Constitution and the rule of law. It showed that nobody was above the law, also not the President. An important aspect of the judgment was that the Concourt had made declaratory orders that both President Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations. And the Concourt found it was duty-bound to rule on that. The court ruled that President Zuma had to personally pay back the money for some of the upgrades, following a determination by the National Treasury. Definite steps to determine how much Zuma should pay for the swimming pool, cattle kraal, chicken run, visitors' centre, and amphitheatre built at Nkandla. The court ruled that the president must reprimand the ministers involved - as he said he would do in a draft order submitted to the court before the hearing in February, Zuma said he was willing to reprimand ministers, in line with the public protector’s remedial action. The Constitutional Court made four orders relating to the repayment of some of the R246m spent on non-security upgrades at Nkandla. Firstly, National Treasury had to determine the reasonable cost of those features; namely the swimming pool, chicken run, cattle kraal, amphitheatre, and visitors’ centre. Secondly, it had to determine how much of this amount Zuma should pay. Treasury then had 60 days to report back to the court with its findings. Finally, Zuma then had 45 days to pay back the money. - President Zuma, the National Assembly, and the Minister of Police had to pay the costs of the application, including the costs of two counsel. The Nkandla matter still haunts pres. Jacob Zuma and Parliament. In December 2017, in an application by the EFF, UDM and COPE, the Constitutional Court found that the National Assembly had failed in its duties by not putting in place processes to hold the president accountable for his failure to implement the remedial action subscribed by the Public Protector in her report on the Nkandla security upgrades. The court found that the National Assembly breached the constitution and ordered it to make rules about the process mentioned in section 89 (1) of the Constitution, namely the process to impeach a president. SASSA CASE, CONCOURT, MARCH 2017 In the Sassa social grants case, the Constitutional Court ordered the Department of Social Development to put systems in place to take over the payment of social grants from Cash Paymaster Services (CPS). This after the court declared the contract with CPS invalid. The department ignored the court’s first order in this regard, and after making a second order, the Constitutional Court felt it necessary to act uncharacteristically and appoint itself as a nanny to oversee the entire process. The department and Sassa was ordered to give the court regular process updates. Since then, Sassa finally, after many false starts, reached a deal with the Post Office to assist in distributing social grants. The court ordered that an inquiry be held into the social grants debacle. The inquiry is ongoing, chaired by retired judge Bernard Ngoepe. The court also ordered Social Development Minister Bathabile Dlamini to personally carry the costs of the case, but she has submitted reasons why she should not be held personally liable. CLARKE 0957 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 11 February 2018 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 27 February 2018 Press Release: From the review of the Public Protector’s State of Capture report, to the Constitutional Court ruling that the National Assembly failed to hold president Jacob Zuma to account, the state is by far the biggest litigant in our courts. At any given time, there are hundreds of ongoing cases against national, provincial and local departments – and in many cases the government keeps losing. Justified litigation, or a taxpayers' burden? Script: VO: Over just 22 days in December, the country’s courts delivered three judgments scathing in their criticism of president Jacob Zuma and parliament. But these were just the latest in a long list. DEVI LINK: Reckless, conflicted, in breach of constitutional obligations -- what does it mean when the courts use these words to describe a sitting president and his Ministers? VO: Political analyst Aubrey Matshiqi. AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: Every time a judgment goes against President Jacob Zuma, including the Nxasana matter, many things come to my mind, but foremost out of them is the extent to which his presidency has compromised our institutions. VO: One of those institutions is the National Prosecuting Authority - and Zuma’s hiring and firing at the NPA led to one of the harshest judgments against him to date. He was heavily criticised for offering Mxolisi Nxasana a R17 million golden handshake to resign as prosecutions boss, and then appointing Shaun Abrahams. DEVI LINK: Judge President of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Dunstan Mlambo ordered that Shaun Abrahams’ appointment was invalid and should be set aside, and that the next National Director of Public Prosecutions should be appointed by the deputy president. (DATE STRAP: North Gauteng High Court, 8 December 2017) UPSOUND JUDGE DUNSTAN MLAMBO: In our view, President Zuma would be clearly conflicted in having to appoint a National Director of Public Prosecutions, given the background to which we have referred, particularly the many criminal charges against him that have not gone away. VO: The corruption charges against Zuma date from the Arms Deal before he became president in 2009, and last year the Supreme Court of Appeal held that Abrahams should consider the charges anew. DEVI LINK: The biggest question now is, what will happen once he’s no longer president -- will he finally have to answer in court to the litany of corruption charges he’s been fighting for a decade? VO: Retired Constitutional Court Justice Johann Kriegler says Judge Mlambo’s judgment was a game changer. JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: It made a credibility finding against the President. Now, that’s the first time that I am aware of that that has been so clearly decided in court. VO: Retired Constitutional Court Justice Zak Yacoob believes cases like these come down to desperate scrambling by the president and his allies. ZAK YACOOB, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: If you want to have an immoral government and a corrupt government every… no effort is lost in preserving that corrupt and immoral government because they won’t give up power and they will use state resources. AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: You can’t appoint Mickey Mouse as your president and expect the state to perform like Albert Einstein. VO: The other two judgments in December both related to Public Protector reports. In the Constitutional Court (DATE STRAP: Constitutional Court, 29 December 2017), 7 judges berated Parliament for failing to hold Zuma to account for his conduct related to the Nkandla report. DEVI LINK: The significant and hard-hitting judgments against the national executive really started with the Nkandla judgment in this court nearly two years ago. It was the first time under our democracy that a court had such harsh words for a president. VO: That was in March 2016, when the country’s highest court ordered Zuma to pay back the money spent on non-security upgrades. (DATE STRAP: Constitutional Court, 31 March 2016) JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: It was the first real show of force, of muscle, by the Constitutional Court in saying to both the President and to Parliament, you’ve not done your job and you've got to do your job. That was a very, very significant case. VO: In December, Judge Mlambo, also sent the president packing when he tried to fight the State of Capture report. Mlambo called the bid ill-advised and reckless. (DATE STRAP: North Gauteng High Court, 13 December 2017) JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: If the courts use such strong language, it is an indication that there’s something wrong. It’s deplorable that such things have to be said but it’s commendable that they are being said. VO: In the NPA case, Judge Mlambo berated Zuma for his tendency to appeal -- “... defending what ultimately turns out – on the president’s own concession – to have been indefensible all along, banking on any advantage that the passage of time may bring.” Zuma, Abrahams and the NPA are all appealing. Of course, the longer a case stays in court, the more expensive it becomes. And ultimately, it’s the taxpayer who coughs up millions. AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: We’re talking about the amount of taxpayers’ monies that had been wasted when actors in the state, including the President have appealed to higher courts, sometimes to defend the indefensible. VO: On any given day, there are hundreds of cases involving government departments in our courts, from claims for medical negligence and unlawful arrest to labour cases. In the last 6 months, the Office of the State Attorney received more than 2700 new cases. The budget for state legal services is R1.2 billion a year. But in high-profile cases, the president, parliament and ministers don’t use the State Attorney’s lawyers -- they hire expensive advocates in private practice. JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: What is disturbing about it, is that many cases where the president personally or the minister personally is involved, the state pays those costs. That is of course wrong. VO: Legal taxation experts say the bill for a team of advocates in a Constitutional Court case will be at least R1 million. This is the bill of a senior advocate who acted in the Constitutional Court in a case about the appointment of former Hawks head Berning Ntlemeza. It comes to just over R1 million. When the state loses, they must not only pay their own legal eagles, but usually also those of their opponents. In the 2016 Nkandla case, there were 11 advocates fighting the state’s case, and the state was also ordered to pay for 4 advocates for the EFF and DA. The cost would have been at least R15 million. ZAK YACOOB, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: It’s a kind of double standards thing. The ANC would say, when they lose cases, people shouldn’t go to court and so on and so on, but they go to court often enough. VO: Sometimes the courts do order government employees to pay the costs out of their own pockets. In December, Judge Mlambo ordered Zuma to pay up himself in both the NPA case and the review of the state capture report. The bill for all those advocates just to appear in the high court, would run to at least R1.9 million. ZAK YACOOB, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: When they bring a case in the High Court and they lose, then go … take six months and go to the Supreme Court of Appeal, take another year and go the Constitutional Court and concede there, maybe in five years’ time, they’ll be ordered to pay. And then Zuma will go to his corrupt contacts who’ll form all sorts of linkages with all sorts of companies, and pay the costs. VO: As South Africa grapples with an economy in trouble, it is untenable to keep paying these bills. The question remains: Where to from here? JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: There has been an over-emphasis of the role of Mr Zuma in the bad place in which we find ourselves. I believe that there is much more involved in the capture of the nation than just Mr Zuma and his close associates. AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: It is disappointing when you hear some ANC leaders saying the National Party was just as bad as if the National Party should be the standard by which we judge ourselves, whereas what we were fighting for is a society that would be the direct opposite, that would be the antithesis, of what apartheid society was. PROMOS 10 secs VO: Recently, government has suffered a series of heavy defeats in the country’s top courts, and no less than three in December. So, who’s paying for these losses? 15 secs VO: What does it mean when the highest courts in the land deliver scathing judgments against the president and his top brass, even calling the president conflicted? JOHANN KRIEGLER, RETIRED CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGE: It made a credibility finding against the President. 15 secs VO: Who pays when the president and government keep suffering significant losses in the country’s courtrooms? AUBREY MATSHIQI, POLITICAL ANALYST: The amount of taxpayers’ monies that had been wasted, sometimes to defend the indefensible.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: What picture emerges from the litany of recent judgments going against the president, his top ministers and parliament? What does it say when our highest courts need to take matters in hand to force the top executive - President Jacob Zuma, his Cabinet, the National Authority of Parliament to do what they are actually just supposed to do being in those positions? Why is it necessary for any political party or labour union or civil society to go to court to ask judges to rule and make it a court order to see change? The last 18 months have seen several judgments going against decisions made by pres. Jacob Zuma, his top ministers and Parliament. In many of these cases, the courts have ordered the president, parliament and ministers to do their jobs - and often even ordered them to pay up for the legal costs too. We sketch the big picture of the cumulative effect of these judgments and look at the implications of such judgments being delivered against the state. With President Jacob Zuma's future seriously hanging in the balance and the President meeting with the the ANC's top six officials over his future this coming weekend, it adds to speculation that President Zuma could be removed as head of state. This is exactly where these judgments delivered against the state are even more significant - because they all happened under Zuma's watch and many were delivered directly against him or against decisions he acted on. We look at some of the major judgments in which the highest levels of the executive, like the Presidency and Parliament, has been lambasted in over the last 18 months and the consequences of these playing out at the moment. In many of these cases, the state has also launched appeal after appeal, driving up the costs even further. We will estimate the costs of these cases to the state, and ultimately to the taxpayer.
